target: AG1’s claim that a national Election Day holiday would remove scheduling barriers and let more Americans vote
objection: A federal holiday does not guarantee paid time off in private-sector jobs, especially for low-income retail and service workers, so many people would still face the same work and lost-wages barrier to voting.

target: AG1’s assumption that a holiday would help low-income workers rather than burden them
objection: If low-income workers still have to work on Election Day, a holiday can leave them with the same scheduling problem plus uncompensated lost time, making the policy potentially disadvantageous for them instead of helpful.

target: AG1’s broader claim that an Election Day holiday is an effective turnout reform
objection: Research suggests that simply making Election Day a holiday is not especially effective at increasing turnout compared with other reforms that directly improve voting access.

target: AG1’s implication that a holiday is the best or sufficient way to improve access
objection: More reliable alternatives exist, such as state laws requiring employer time off to vote and automatic voter registration, so a national holiday is not the most dependable reform.

target: AG2’s claim that a federal holiday would not reliably provide paid voting time for low-income workers
objection: On federal holidays, many schools close and many workplaces reduce hours or close, so a national holiday would make Election Day less like a normal school/work day for many people, including many low-income workers.

target: AG2’s argument that the real barrier is still work schedules and unpaid time off
objection: If Election Day is treated as a non-working or non-class day, voters can vote without needing extra time off or missed wages, so the holiday directly reduces the scheduling barrier rather than merely swapping one form of leave problem for another.

target: AG2’s claim that low-income workers would be disadvantaged by a holiday
objection: Because low-income voters are especially affected by missing work and losing pay, a holiday would lessen that burden rather than worsen it by reducing the need to miss work or class on Election Day.

target: AG2’s claim that Election Day should not be a holiday because other reforms exist
objection: Even if other voting-access reforms are also needed, that does not mean Election Day should not be made a holiday; multiple reforms can be complementary.

target: AG2’s claim that turnout research undercuts holiday proposals
objection: A policy can be combined with other reforms, so evidence that a holiday alone is not sufficient does not by itself show that the holiday should be rejected.

target: AG2’s claim that weekend/holiday election timing is not a good model
objection: The fact that 27 of 36 OECD countries hold elections on weekends or holidays suggests that such timing is workable and widely used in comparable democracies.

target: AG2’s analogy to private employers not being required to give paid holidays
objection: Many low-income workers are affected not only by employer-paid leave, but also by school and care responsibilities that a holiday would reduce by making the day less like a normal workday.

target: AG1’s claim that schools and workplaces usually reduce hours on holidays, so a holiday would help voting
objection: The existence of a federal holiday does not ensure that private employers will reduce hours or close, so many workers may still have to work on Election Day.

target: AG1’s broader claim that a holiday would meaningfully improve access for low-income workers
objection: Because federal holidays do not mandate paid time off in the private sector, low-income workers can still face rigid schedules and may not get meaningful relief from the policy.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday would address the main access problem
objection: The real barriers to turnout also include pre-Election Day problems like registration and keeping registration current, which a holiday does not fix.

target: AG1’s reliance on civic symbolism
objection: Making voting feel celebratory does not address concrete administrative barriers, so it is not a substitute for reforms that directly improve access.

target: AG2’s suggestion that pre-Election Day administrative barriers make a holiday ineffective
objection: A holiday can still reduce day-of scheduling barriers even if it does not solve every administrative problem, so it should not be dismissed for failing to do everything at once.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday would not help low-income workers
objection: If schools and workplaces operate on holiday schedules, low-income workers can have practical access to vote because the day is less likely to require normal attendance.

target: AG2’s argument that low-income workers still face rigid schedules on holidays
objection: A national holiday reduces the need to be at school or work during voting hours, which lowers the practical day-of barrier for low-income workers even if paid leave is not guaranteed everywhere.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday is not enough because of pre-Election Day eligibility issues
objection: A reform does not need to fix every barrier to be worthwhile; even if administrative hurdles remain, removing the day-of scheduling barrier still expands access.

target: AG2’s claim that the holiday would not reliably help voters on Election Day
objection: If schools and workplaces are less likely to run normally on Election Day, then the scheduling overlap between availability and voting hours is reduced, which makes voting more feasible.

target: AG2’s implication that celebration is merely symbolic
objection: Reframing voting as a civic celebration can elevate the perceived importance of participation and therefore increase civic engagement.

target: AG2’s claim that pre-Election Day reforms make a holiday unnecessary
objection: An Election Day holiday can complement other reforms like automatic voter registration; the existence of other reforms does not negate the value of reducing day-of barriers.

target: AG2’s argument that turnout barriers are mainly pre-Election Day and not day-of scheduling
objection: A major barrier remains being unable to be free during voting hours because of school or work, so reducing the overlap between attendance obligations and voting time still matters.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday does not address administrative hurdles and therefore is insufficient
objection: A holiday can still improve access by directly reducing the time-of-day conflict that prevents many voters from participating, even if it does not solve registration problems.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday would not meaningfully help low-income workers
objection: Low-income workers often have less schedule flexibility, so reducing the need to be at work during voting hours would expand their practical ability to vote.

target: AG2’s claim that election access reforms should focus only on administrative barriers
objection: A holiday can complement administrative reforms by removing major scheduling barriers, so it is still substantively valuable even alongside automatic voter registration.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday is not a workable election model
objection: The fact that many OECD countries hold elections on weekends or holidays shows that this is a feasible and commonly used approach.
